title: An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a transferable way to predict turbulent engineering flows accurately at a computational cost suitable for design. Given an unfamiliar geometry and operating conditions, it would predict forces, flow separation and transport without requiring case-specific adjustment against experimental results. Heat transfer and scalar mixing are intended parts of this broader capability, but would require validation beyond the incompressible momentum closures emphasized in the supplied source.

The central difficulty is representing turbulent motion that a practical calculation cannot resolve directly. A closure supplies the effects of those unresolved motions on the quantities being calculated. Existing closures use approximations and calibration that can work well in particular regimes but transfer poorly when flow structures, geometry or Reynolds number change. The desired advance would make that transfer reliable while retaining useful accuracy and manageable computational cost.

Conceptual scope: this is a goal for tractable engineering prediction, rather than a claim that fluid mechanics lacks governing equations. It is distinct from proving mathematical regularity of the Navier–Stokes equations. The innovation could involve improved closures, methods that resolve selected turbulent scales, or a combination of physical theory and computation; the concept does not prescribe one implementation.

significance.text: If achieved, reliable prediction outside familiar calibration cases would make simulation a stronger basis for engineering decisions. Designers could assess how changes in geometry or operating conditions affect loads, separation and transport with greater confidence. Girimaji's discussion of methods that resolve coherent scales while modeling the remainder explains the relevant tradeoff: predictive improvement must come at a cost compatible with practical design work.

Conditional engineering consequences: aircraft, turbines, pumps and heat exchangers could require fewer experimental iterations if simulations reliably identified promising designs and operating limits before hardware was built. Better prediction could also support improvements in efficiency, cooling and mixing. These are plausible downstream benefits of the hypothetical capability, not demonstrated outcomes of the supplied evidence; their extent would depend on application-specific validation and on the other constraints governing each machine.

Limits of the impact: predictive understanding would not itself suppress turbulence, provide a flow-control mechanism or guarantee an optimal machine. Reliable momentum predictions would also not automatically establish reliable thermal or mixing predictions. Experiments would remain important for validation and for effects outside the demonstrated scope, so reduced dependence on full-scale testing should be treated as a conditional possibility rather than an assured replacement of testing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reliable representation of unresolved turbulence that remains accurate in unfamiliar practical flows without extensive ad hoc modification. Improving agreement with a few calibration statistics is insufficient if the model does not capture the mechanisms that determine behavior under changed conditions. The supplied perspective connects this transfer problem to flow-dependent coherent structures, geometry and Reynolds number, rather than treating all turbulence as one statistically interchangeable phenomenon.

Concrete physical barriers include nonlinear advection, nonlocal pressure effects and dependence on flow history. These features make it difficult to infer the needed turbulent stresses from only the local, instantaneous quantities available to a simple closure. The paper distinguishes regimes in which established Reynolds-averaged models perform well from flows with strong coherent structures in which traditional models without memory can perform poorly. That distinction matters: success in a comparatively simple regime does not establish transfer to structurally different turbulence.

The engineering barrier is to preserve the relevant physics without making computation prohibitively expensive. Direct numerical simulation resolves turbulent motion in detail, but computational limits restrict its practical reach. Methods that resolve selected scales and model the rest offer a compromise, yet still face the problem of choosing and representing unresolved dynamics reliably. Machine learning must address these physical and generalization constraints; fitting available data alone does not establish predictive performance on unseen flows.

Scope requirement: extending the innovation to heat transfer, scalar mixing, separated flows and additional multiphysics requires explicit demonstrations in those regimes. The supplied evidence does not establish that one successful incompressible momentum closure would solve these extensions, nor does it separately document separation-specific performance.

current_state.text: The verified historical assessment comes from Girimaji's December 2023 arXiv version 1. It describes useful established turbulence models and the role of direct numerical simulation data for selected flows. In particular, it identifies good Reynolds-averaged model performance in the near-equilibrium homogeneous regime discussed in section 5.1. This is evidence of useful capability within a specified regime, not a comprehensive benchmark of practical turbulent-flow prediction.

The same perspective reports that progress toward predictive machine-learned Reynolds-averaged closures had been slower than anticipated. It attributes the difficulty to nonlinear, nonlocal and memory effects, and discusses limitations in transferring models to unseen flows. Sections 5.1, 5.3 and 6 more directly support the generalization and practical-modeling assessment, while section 2 supplies the underlying physics. The source is a perspective, not a demonstration of a broadly transferable solution.

The supplied evidence contains no freshness search establishing the field's status as of November 1, 2026. It therefore supports a dated account of capabilities and barriers, but cannot establish whether a later advance has resolved some of them. It also supplies neither a broad quantitative DNS validation survey nor separate evidence for the earlier emphasis on separated-flow prediction. These evidence limits leave those questions open; they do not show that a particular result is false.

Access and version limits affect the bibliographic interpretation. The research associates the work with a 2024 New Journal of Physics article, but the supplied review verifies the December 2023 arXiv text and notes that its title differs from the supplied journal metadata. The publisher fetch was blocked, so the journal version and DOI were not verified. The retained HTML is an abstract page; the PDF text includes the main discussion and references but substitutes external-image notices for figures. Those missing figures limit completeness without preventing assessment of the textual arguments used here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: blindly predict predeclared force coefficients and a principal heat-transfer or mixing measure across multiple withheld attached and separated flows. Include engineering Reynolds numbers beyond the reach of comparable direct numerical simulations, and prohibit case-specific retuning after reference results become available. The test should establish what was withheld and how the evaluation cases differ from the model's calibration experience.
completion_criteria.label: Blindly predict force coefficients and transport across withheld engineering flows

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accuracy criterion: errors within 5% of experimental reference values would be a demanding initial target, not an established completion standard. Predeclare the error definitions, the relevant operating points and experimental uncertainties. Where a reference value approaches zero, use a predeclared absolute tolerance so that a relative-error percentage does not become misleading or undefined.
completion_criteria.label: Predeclare error criteria and near-zero tolerances with experimental uncertainties

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practicality and reproducibility requirements: specify computational budgets and hardware before evaluation, report actual resource use, and provide enough implementation and case-definition detail for independent replication. Multiple geometries and independently performed evaluations should test whether the result transfers beyond one favorable configuration. Report failures and sensitivity to inputs alongside successful predictions.
completion_criteria.label: Report computational costs and enable independent replication across geometries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary: a finite benchmark can establish demonstrated breadth within tested regimes, not literal universality. A convincing result should identify its validated ranges of geometry, Reynolds number, flow behavior and transported quantities. Momentum, separation, heat transfer, mixing and additional coupled physics should receive distinct validation where claimed, with remaining limitations stated explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: State validated regimes and limitations for each claimed capability

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-03, “Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting,” and MEC-14, “Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods,” could benefit from improved predictions of fluid losses or heat transfer where those processes govern performance. MEC-01 supplies a potential analysis capability; it does not establish economical low-temperature heat conversion or the efficiency, cost and retention performance required for mechanical storage.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” share interests in friction, losses or predictive transfer across operating conditions. Fluid behavior could intersect with these concepts in lubricated contacts, but turbulent-flow prediction does not by itself explain evolving contact geometry, wear or sustained superlubricity. MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” could use better fluid-load estimates in some applications, while its required material resistance remains a separate capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-05, “Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms,” MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” and MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” concern creating or selecting mechanical behavior. MEC-01 could support their design when fluid loads, cooling or fluid actuation matter, but reliable analysis does not supply reconfiguration, muscle-like actuation, structural growth or automatic mechanism synthesis.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-06, “Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis,” MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” and MEC-09, “Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock,” primarily concern fabrication, material performance or production capability. Their connection to MEC-01 is indirect, through possible fluid-handling or thermal-design needs. Each remains a distinct innovation with completion requirements that turbulent-flow prediction would not satisfy.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-01 and its title while expanding the explanation of closures, transfer to unfamiliar flows and computational practicality.
change_log.reason: The research and review support a coherent engineering-prediction concept whose identity does not depend on every supporting assertion being established.

change_log.change: Integrated nonlinear advection, nonlocal pressure, memory effects and flow-dependent coherent structures into the explanation of the missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why calibration success and data fitting do not necessarily produce transferable predictions.

change_log.change: Dated the supported assessment to December 2023 arXiv version 1 and qualified the supplied 2024 journal attribution.
change_log.reason: The review verified the preprint, while publisher access was blocked and the journal metadata and DOI were not verified.

change_log.change: Narrowed the description of established-model performance to the regimes supported by the review and removed an unqualified present-day assessment.
change_log.reason: The evidence is a dated perspective, provides no 2026 freshness search and does not separately substantiate separation-specific performance.

change_log.change: Separated intended heat-transfer and mixing capability from the source's primary treatment of incompressible momentum closures.
change_log.reason: Thermal, scalar and additional multiphysics performance require their own validation.

change_log.change: Retained reduced experimental iteration and machinery improvements as conditional consequences, with explicit prediction-versus-control limits.
change_log.reason: These are plausible benefits of the hypothetical breakthrough, not outcomes demonstrated by the supplied source.

change_log.change: Refined the proposed benchmark with predeclared observables, computational budgets, uncertainty treatment, error definitions and absolute tolerances near zero.
change_log.reason: These additions make the proposed 5% target interpretable without presenting it as an established standard.

change_log.change: Added independent replication and explicit boundaries on what finite testing can establish.
change_log.reason: Multiple successful cases demonstrate breadth within tested regimes rather than universal predictive capability.

change_log.reason: The record should remain transparent about evidence access and preserve distinct innovation identities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish the field's status as of November 1, 2026 or document subsequent advances.
The relationship between the verified December 2023 arXiv version and the supplied 2024 journal title and DOI remains unverified.
The retained PDF text omits figures; their contribution cannot be assessed from the supplied review.
Broad quantitative performance across practical flows, particularly separated flows, heat transfer, scalar mixing and additional multiphysics, is not established by the supplied perspective.
The proposed benchmark still requires specific cases, operating ranges, computational budgets, error aggregation rules and absolute tolerances before execution; the 5% target remains a proposal.

brief.title: Reliable predictions of turbulent flow for design
possible: Engineers could predict how air or water behaves around an unfamiliar design before building it. Simulations would reliably calculate forces, flow peeling away from surfaces, heat transfer and mixing without adjusting the model to match experiments for each new case.
why: Designers of aircraft, turbines, pumps and heat exchangers could compare shapes and operating conditions with greater confidence. Reliable simulations could reduce experimental iterations and help improve efficiency, cooling and mixing.

sources.showed: This perspective explains why models of unresolved turbulent motion struggle with unfamiliar flows. Pressure effects from elsewhere in the flow and dependence on past motion make simple local predictions difficult.
sources.cited_for: It explains the physical barriers to predictions that remain reliable when geometry and flow conditions change.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a method that predicts unfamiliar engineering flows accurately at a practical cost.

sources.who: Chenyu Wu, Shaoguang Zhang, Changxin Guo and Yufei Zhang
sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reports improved predictions where flow peels away from surfaces. Its model carries information along the flow and matched or beat local correction models on all tested cases outside its training set.
sources.quote:
In all tested 
cases, the 𝛽-Transport model yields smaller or equal prediction errors compared to those from 
classic local data-driven turbulence models using algebraic relations for 𝛽.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates improved transfer to unfamiliar shapes and flow conditions in the tested flows.
sources.not_established: These tests do not establish broad blind accuracy, independent replication or reliable heat-transfer and mixing predictions.

sources.who: K. Goc, S. T. Bose and P. Moin
sources.showed: The team simulated an aircraft model in landing configuration by calculating larger turbulent motions and modeling smaller ones. Predicted lift agreed well with wind-tunnel measurements near maximum lift.
sources.quote:
The lift curve pre dicted by WMLES is
in good agreement with experimental force balance measurements obtained near stall,
as shown in Figure 6.
sources.cited_for: It shows that resolving selected turbulent motions can predict forces on a complex aircraft configuration.
sources.not_established: Agreement on this aircraft configuration does not establish reliable transfer across designs within practical computing budgets.

shown: Wu and colleagues report better predictions on unfamiliar separated flows, where fluid peels away from a surface. Goc and colleagues reproduced lift near its maximum on an aircraft model in landing configuration. These demonstrate parts of the capability.
missing: Reliable predictions across unfamiliar practical flows still need to succeed without adjustments based on each case's experimental results.
The relevant effects of unresolved motion need to be retained within computing budgets suitable for design.
Heat transfer and mixing need their own demonstrations; accurate force predictions do not establish either.
Independent teams need to reproduce broad performance across different geometries.

milestones.label: Blind predictions across unfamiliar engineering flows
milestones.explanation: Blind tests would have to predict forces and heat transfer or mixing across withheld attached and separated flows too demanding to simulate in full detail, without case-specific retuning. This would test transfer beyond calibration.

milestones.label: Accuracy judged against declared experimental tolerances
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to declare error rules and experimental uncertainties, with absolute tolerances near zero; 5% error is a proposed target. This would make accuracy claims meaningful.

milestones.label: Practical costs and independently reproduced results
milestones.explanation: Teams would have to declare hardware and budgets, report actual costs, failures and input sensitivity, and enable independent replication across geometries. This would test practical use and reproducibility.

milestones.label: Clear boundaries for every validated capability
milestones.explanation: Results would have to define tested shapes and flow conditions, separately validating forces, separation, heat transfer, mixing and coupled effects where claimed. This would establish demonstrated breadth and its limits.

uncertain: How broadly can successful models transfer when flow geometry, speed and organized turbulent patterns change?
Which benchmark cases, computing budgets and error rules would establish useful engineering reliability?
Is the proposed accuracy target appropriate across the different forces and transport quantities being predicted?
